q-112612:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-4{z}^{2}-16z-7) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 4{z}^{2}+16z+7 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{z}^{2}+16z+7 & =0 \\ 4{z}^{2}+16z & =-7 \\ 4({z}^{2}+4z) & =-7 \\ 4[{z}^{2}+2\cdot 2\cdot z+{(2)}^{2}-{(2)}^{2}] & =-7 \\ 4[{(z+2)}^{2}-4] & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(z+2)}^{2}-4\cdot 4 & =-7 \\ 4{(z+2)}^{2}-16 & =-7 \\ 4{(z+2)}^{2} & =-7+16 \\ 4{(z+2)}^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=2.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(z+2)}^{2} & =9 \\ {(z+2)}^{2} & =\frac{9}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(z+2)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}} \\ |z+2| & =\frac{3}{2} \\ z+2 & =\pm \frac{3}{2} \\ z & =-2\pm \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =-2-\frac{3}{2}=-\frac{7}{2} \\ z & =-2+\frac{3}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $z=-\frac{7}{2}$ and $z=-\frac{1}{2}.$

q-142142:
First, we recall the difference formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

Applying the difference formula for cosine with $u=x$ and $v={210}^{∘},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-{210}^{∘}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡{210}^{∘}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡{210}^{∘} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

q-161109:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}bc\operatorname{sin}⁡A,
$$

where $∠A$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB=6\text{ cm}, \\ b & =AC, \\ m∠A & ={45}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},
$$

we can calculate $b=AC,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \frac{21\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot 6\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘} \\ \frac{21\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot 6\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{21\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}\,b}{2} \\ \frac{21\cancel{\sqrt{2}}}{\cancel{2}} & =\frac{3\cancel{\sqrt{2}}\,b}{\cancel{2}} \\ 3b & =21 \\ b & =7\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $AC=7\,\text{cm}.$

q-72213:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+{y}^{3}=2{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y))+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}) \\ [x(\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)]+3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2} \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+3{y}^{2}) & =6{x}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{6{x}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+3{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

q-555:
The denominator is $2-\text{i}$ and its conjugate is $2+\text{i}.$ We multiply both the numerator and the denominator by $2+\text{i},$ so that the denominator turns into a real number:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{i}}{2-\text{i}} & =\frac{\text{i}}{2-\text{i}}\cdot \frac{2+\text{i}}{2+\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{2\text{i}+{\text{i}}^{2}}{{2}^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-1+2\text{i}}{{2}^{2}-(-1)} \\  & =\frac{-1+2\text{i}}{4+1} \\  & =\frac{-1+2\text{i}}{5}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the denominator is a real number, we can write the complex number in the form $a+b\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{-1+2\text{i}}{5}=-\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-16433:
The denominator is $-5+4\text{i}$ and its conjugate is $-5-4\text{i}.$ We multiply both the numerator and the denominator by $-5-4\text{i},$ so that the denominator turns into a real number:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{9\text{i}}{-5+4\text{i}} & =\frac{9\text{i}}{-5+4\text{i}}\cdot \frac{-5-4\text{i}}{-5-4\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{-45\text{i}-36{\text{i}}^{2}}{{5}^{2}-{4}^{2}{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-45\text{i}-36(-1)}{{5}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{36-45\text{i}}{25+16} \\  & =\frac{36-45\text{i}}{41}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the denominator is a real number, we can write the complex number in the form $a+b\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{36-45\text{i}}{41}=\frac{36}{41}-\frac{45}{41}\text{i}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-74648:
The denominator is $-3+2\text{i}$ and its conjugate is $-3-2\text{i}.$ We multiply both the numerator and the denominator by $-3-2\text{i},$ so that the denominator turns into a real number:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{-3+2\text{i}} & =\frac{9}{-3+2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{-3-2\text{i}}{-3-2\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{-27-18\text{i}}{9+6\text{i}-6\text{i}-4{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-27-18\text{i}}{9-4(-1)} \\  & =\frac{-27-18\text{i}}{9+4} \\  & =\frac{-27-18\text{i}}{13}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the denominator is a real number, we can write the complex number in the form $a+b\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{-27-18\text{i}}{13}=-\frac{27}{13}-\frac{18}{13}\text{i}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-167677:
Here, the denominator is the imaginary number $5\text{i}.$ Note that this can be written as $0+5\text{i},$ so the conjugate is $0-5\text{i},$ or simply $-5\text{i}.$

So, we multiply both the numerator and the denominator by $-5\text{i},$ so that the denominator turns into a real number:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5+2\text{i}}{5\text{i}} & =\frac{5+2\text{i}}{5\text{i}}\cdot \frac{-5\text{i}}{-5\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{-25\text{i}-10{\text{i}}^{2}}{-25{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-25\text{i}-10(-1)}{-25(-1)} \\  & =\frac{10-25\text{i}}{25}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the denominator is a real number, we can write the complex number in the form $a+b\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{10-25\text{i}}{25} & =\frac{10}{25}-\frac{25}{25}\text{i} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}-\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

q-81863:
The range of the function $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is $y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

Horizontal and vertical shifts and stretches do not affect the range of a logarithmic function.

Therefore, the range of the given function is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ and the function has no maximum value.

q-166549:
To find the root of $f(x)$, we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
{log}_{2}⁡(4-2x)+1=0
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(4-2x)+1 & =0 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(4-2x) & =-1 \\ {2}^{{log}_{2}⁡(4-2x)} & ={2}^{-1} \\ 4-2x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ -2x & =-\frac{7}{2} \\ x & =\frac{7}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the root of $f(x)$ is $x=\frac{7}{4}.$

q-102616:
We differentiate $v(t)$ to calculate $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+4t) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1+4 \\  & =5+\operatorname{ln}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the time when the acceleration is $a=6,$ we substitute this into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =5+\operatorname{ln}⁡t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t & =1 \\ {e}^{(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)} & ={e}^{1} \\ t & =e\end{aligned}
$$

Then, to calculate the velocity at time $t=e,$ we substitute this into the equation for the velocity:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(e) & =(e\operatorname{ln}⁡e+4e) \\  & =e(1)+4e \\  & =5e\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity when $a=6\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}$ is $5e\text{ m/s}.$

q-2361:
We differentiate $v(t)$ to calculate $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{2}-16t+15) \\  & =8t-16\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the time when the acceleration is $a=0,$ we substitute this into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =8t-16 \\ 8t & =16 \\ t & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, to calculate the velocity at time $t=2,$ we substitute this into the equation for the velocity:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =4(2)^{2}-16(2)+15 \\  & =16-32+15 \\  & =-1\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity when $a=0\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}$ is $-1\,\text{m/s}.$

q-8431:
First, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=-\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $x=-\frac{\pi }{3}$ is not in the range $0\le x<2\pi .$ To get the first solution that's within the required range, we need to find an angle that's coterminal with $-\frac{\pi }{3}.$ To do this, we simply add $2\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-\frac{\pi }{3}+2\pi =\frac{5\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Our first solution lies in the fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13951962/assets/0716b8ab50e525f453ae8bc690d404a150f2da98f0a90b6c8856ae9925e7c515.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=\frac{4\pi }{3},\frac{5\pi }{3}.$

Finally, 

$$
{x}_{1}{x}_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{3}\cdot \frac{4\pi }{3}=\frac{20{\pi }^{2}}{9}.
$$

q-120835:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{5}{8})=38.682{…}^{∘}≈{38.68}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${38.68}^{∘}$ lies inside the range, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={38.68}^{∘}.$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={38.68}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the second quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={38.68}^{∘}.$

q-8577:
First, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{1}{6})=-0.167\,448…≈-0.167\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-0.167$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=-0.167\,4.$

Our first solution lies in the fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=0.167\,4.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=0.167\,4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13951962/assets/f6f08d799cd2d2e80494d94cc3b18a61f73227b88b25d79c926d65e161d4ce3a.png)

A second solution $X$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, and we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +0.167\,4 \\  & ≈3.309\,0\end{aligned}
$$

However, this value is not in the required domain. To get the second solution ${x}_{2}$ that's within the given domain, we simply subtract $2\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}=X-2\pi  & ≈3.309-2\pi ≈-2.974\,2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=(-0.167\,4)\cdot (-2.974\,2)≈0.5,
$$

rounded to $1$ decimal place.

q-120234:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{2})^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2+2} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{-\sqrt{2}})| \\  & =|-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the second quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $\pi ,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are  $(2,\frac{3\pi }{4}).$
